records.title: Textile Upcycling, Family Empowerment and Circular Livelihoods in Jos North, Nigeria: Empirical Evidence from 100 Upcycling Households
records.author_source_text: Akila, L. K.¹* · Agbo, D. A.²; ¹ Department of Home and Rural Economics, Plateau State College of Agriculture, Garkawa, Plateau State, Nigeria. ² Department of Home Science and Management, Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi, Benue State, Nigeria.; *Corresponding author: lydiaakila1@gmail.com · Co-author: drdianadagbo@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Textile upcycling converts discarded or surplus fabrics into products of renewed or higher use value and can link household livelihood strategies with circular-economy objectives. Objective: This study examined upcycling participation, family empowerment, income effects, environmental benefits and practical constraints among families engaged in textile upcycling in Jos North, Plateau State, Nigeria. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 100 families purposefully selected from a field-identified population of 312 families involved in upcycling activities around Katako, Terminus and adjoining Jos North communities. Data were collected in person with the Upcycling and Family Empowerment Questionnaire and analysed with percentages, descriptive comparison, Pearson correlation and an independent-samples t-test. Results: Participation increased from low (20%) to medium (50%) and high (80%) levels alongside progressively more complex activities, from scrap use and stuffing to garment transformation, household products and recovery of buttons, zippers and trims. Reported family-income increases were +10%, +25% and +50% across the low, medium and high participation levels, respectively. The principal barriers were lack of tools/equipment (30%), insufficient training/skills (20%) and limited market access (15%). Upcycling participation was strongly associated with family empowerment (r=.75, p<.01; derived 95% CI .65-.82). The environmental hypothesis was also supported (t=2.56, p<.05), indicating greater waste reduction/resource recovery among more active upcycling families. Conclusion: In Jos North, textile upcycling operates simultaneously as a material-circulation practice and a household livelihood strategy. Its expansion, however, depends on skills, equipment, product-quality development, market access and supportive circular-economy institutions. The evidence supports integrating household upcycling into vocational training, microenterprise support and locally grounded textile-waste strategies while avoiding causal claims that exceed the cross-sectional design.
records.keywords: textile upcycling; circular economy; family empowerment; household livelihoods; textile waste; sustainable fashion; resource recovery; Jos North; Plateau State; Nigeria

records.title: Digital Transformation in Clothing Technology: Awareness, Practical Adoption and Barriers to Computer-Aided Design among Tailors in Jos Metropolis, Nigeria
records.author_source_text: Akila, L. K.¹* · Anisah, Jacks Zongoro²; ¹ Department of Home and Rural Economics, Plateau State College of Agriculture, Garkawa, Plateau State, Nigeria. ² Federal College of Education (Technical), Gombe, Gombe State, Nigeria.; *Corresponding author: lydiaakila1@gmail.com · Co-author: ajzongoro@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Computer-aided design (CAD) has become integral to contemporary apparel design, pattern engineering, grading, specification development and digitally mediated production, yet adoption within informal tailoring enterprises can lag behind awareness. Objective: This study assessed awareness, practical use and barriers to CAD adoption among tailors in Jos Metropolis, Plateau State, Nigeria, and interpreted the findings within current clothing-technology and vocational-skills evidence. Methods: A descriptive survey design was used. A structured questionnaire was administered to a purposive sample of 150 tailors in Jos Metropolis. The analysis used descriptive percentages; two additional descriptive indicators—the awareness–use gap and use-to-awareness ratio—were calculated directly from the reported percentages. Results: CAD awareness was 68.4%, whereas only 18.2% of respondents reported practical use of CAD for pattern drafting and clothing-design work. The resulting awareness–use gap was 50.2 percentage points, and practical use represented approximately 26.6% of the reported awareness level. The leading barriers were the high cost of computer hardware/software (82.5%), epileptic power supply (76.0%) and lack of technical training (64.3%). These results indicate that knowledge of CAD is substantially more widespread than the capability to integrate it into routine tailoring practice. Conclusion: Digital transformation in the Jos tailoring sector is constrained by a combined affordability–infrastructure–skills problem rather than by awareness alone. Practical adoption requires shared or subsidised digital-fashion infrastructure, reliable power, modular hands-on CAD training and integration of digital pattern-making into informal apprenticeship and vocational education. The study provides locally grounded evidence for a staged transition from CAD awareness to routine, productivity-oriented digital clothing practice.

records.title: Security Challenges and Principals' Management Strategies in North-Central Nigerian Secondary Schools
records.author_source_text: Wilfred Ogbu
records.abstract: Background: Security threats can disrupt attendance, teaching, learning and school administration, while principals are expected to coordinate preventive, protective, detective and response functions within constrained local environments. Objective: This study examined prevalent security challenges in public senior secondary schools in three North-Central Nigerian states and assessed the effectiveness of principals' security-management strategies. Methods: The source manuscript reports a descriptive correlational survey of 45 schools drawn from a population of 894 public senior secondary schools in Benue, Kogi and Nasarawa. Respondents comprised 45 principals, 375 teachers and 384 students. Three four-point questionnaires were used, with reported reliability coefficients of 0.73–0.79. Descriptive statistics and ANOVA were reported at the 0.05 level. Results: The overall security-challenge mean was 2.80 (SD=0.86). Violence (M=3.06), kidnapping/abduction (M=3.04) and communal clashes (M=2.93) were the highest-rated threats. State-level challenge means were Nasarawa 2.93, Kogi 2.65 and Benue 2.57, with a reported significant difference (F=3.689, p=.033). Principals were rated effective in safety programmes (M=2.71), asset protection (M=2.67) and detective strategies (M=2.60), but ineffective in threat prevention (M=2.43) and emergency response (M=2.20). State differences were reported only for asset-protection strategy (F=3.293, p=.038). Conclusion: The evidence indicates a high-threat environment combined with a management gap in prevention and emergency response. The publication update preserves the source statistics without re-estimation and situates the findings within Nigeria's current safe-schools policy framework.
records.keywords: school security; principals; security management; kidnapping; emergency response; secondary schools; North-Central Nigeria; educational administration

records.title: Artificial Intelligence and Smart Border Surveillance for Intellectual Property Rights Enforcement at Nigeria’s Land Borders: A Critical Evidence Review and Responsible Implementation Framework
records.author_source_text: AMENGER, Gbaden; Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria
records.abstract: Background: Counterfeit and pirated trade undermines intellectual property rights (IPR), consumer safety, legitimate enterprise and revenue administration. Border enforcement is becoming harder as illicit trade fragments into small consignments and adapts to complex logistics. Objective: This article critically reviews the evidence for artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics and smart border-surveillance technologies in strengthening IPR enforcement at Nigeria’s land borders and develops a legally bounded implementation framework. Review approach: A structured critical review prioritized official evidence from the World Customs Organization (WCO), World Trade Organization (WTO), OECD/EUIPO, Nigeria Customs Service (NCS), Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) and African Union, supplemented by peer-reviewed customs-risk, African surveillance and IPR-enforcement scholarship published principally from 2020 to August 2026. Synthesis: OECD/EUIPO estimates place global counterfeit and pirated trade at about USD 467 billion in 2021, equivalent to 2.3% of global imports; shipments of fewer than ten items accounted for 79% of customs seizures in 2020–2021, intensifying selectivity pressures. WCO guidance identifies AI/ML, data analytics and cloud technologies as high-interest Customs technologies but stresses data governance, interoperability, cybersecurity, cost-benefit analysis, workforce capability, MLOps, fairness and transparency. Nigeria has moved beyond conceptual readiness: NCS modernization plans include AI-supported risk management, data analytics and geospatial surveillance, while a 2026 Nigeria–Benin operation demonstrated operational use of geospatial intelligence, drones, shared communications and risk profiling. For IPR enforcement, however, technology must be integrated with TRIPS-compliant border procedures, rights-holder product intelligence, human adjudication and data-protection safeguards. Conclusion: The strongest policy case is for phased, evidence-gated adoption rather than technology-first procurement. A Nigerian smart-IPR border architecture should combine reliable Customs data, rights-holder authentication, risk analytics, geospatial targeting and non-intrusive inspection with human review, auditable decisions, privacy-by-design and cross-border cooperation.
records.keywords: artificial intelligence; smart customs; intellectual property rights; counterfeiting; Nigeria Customs Service; border surveillance; geospatial intelligence; customs risk management; responsible AI; trade facilitation

records.title: From Risk Profiles to Counterfeit Interception: AI-Enabled Customs Risk Targeting, Geospatial Intelligence and Non-Intrusive Inspection at Nigeria’s Land Borders
records.author_source_text: AMENGER, Gbaden; Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria
records.abstract: Background: Customs administrations must identify high-risk consignments while allowing compliant trade to move with minimal delay. At Nigeria’s land borders, porous routes, infrastructure constraints, fragmented data and high inspection demands make this selectivity problem particularly acute. Objective: This review examines the operational evidence for AI/ML risk targeting, anomaly detection, geospatial intelligence (GEOINT), AI-assisted non-intrusive inspection (NII) and product-authentication systems, and proposes a performance-assured detection architecture for counterfeit and other IPR-infringing goods. Review approach: Current WCO, WTO, NCS and OECD/EUIPO evidence through August 2026 was synthesized with peer-reviewed Customs risk-management and AI literature. Synthesis: International practice supports a layered model in which structured declaration data, trader history, seizure outcomes and rights-holder alerts feed risk analytics; GEOINT directs attention to spatial hotspots; NII and computer vision support cargo examination; and product-authentication platforms support IPR-specific verification. Nigeria has relevant operational foundations. NCS has documented GEOINT use for illicit-route detection and corridor monitoring, while the 2026 Nigeria–Benin Operation GEOCONTROL used GIS/GEOINT, drones, risk profiling and near-real-time information exchange and recorded 37 seizures during an eight-day operation. Internationally, China Customs has deployed AI-assisted inspection-image analysis at scale, demonstrating technical feasibility but not automatic transferability to Nigeria. The review argues that model quality must be measured with enforcement and facilitation metrics together: precision, recall, calibration, false-positive inspections, clearance time, robustness across border posts and commodities, human override, cybersecurity and cost per actionable hit. Conclusion: A Nigerian smart-border detection system should be multi-modal, human-in-the-loop and locally validated. The operational goal is not maximum automation but better allocation of scarce inspection resources with transparent evidence, continuous monitoring and legally defensible officer decisions.
records.keywords: customs risk management; artificial intelligence; anomaly detection; geospatial intelligence; non-intrusive inspection; computer vision; counterfeiting; intellectual property enforcement; Nigeria; smart borders

records.title: Resilient Hybrid Power Architecture for 24/7 Nigeria Customs Land-Border Operations: Grid, Solar PV, Battery Storage and Generator Coordination
records.author_source_text: AMENGER, Gbaden; Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria; Officer-in-Charge (Electricity), Idiroko Barracks, Ogun I Area Command
records.abstract: Background: Nigeria Customs land-border commands increasingly depend on continuous electricity for communications, ICT, access control, lighting, electronic documentation, surveillance and, where deployed, non-intrusive inspection and other smart-border technologies. Yet national-grid variability and local distribution constraints make generator dependence a persistent operational risk. Objective: This review synthesizes Nigerian power-sector evidence, Customs modernization requirements and microgrid-resilience literature to develop a practical hybrid energy framework for 24/7 border operations. Review approach: Official evidence from NERC, the Nigeria Energy Transition Plan, World Bank distributed-energy programmes, Nigeria Customs Service and World Customs Organization guidance was integrated with peer-reviewed literature on solar-battery-diesel microgrids, battery storage, resilience, energy management and protection through August 2026. Synthesis: NERC reported that average available grid-connected generation fell from 5,400.38 MW in 2025/Q4 to 4,457.96 MW in 2026/Q1, while Q1 2026 recorded one total and one partial system collapse. A border command should therefore treat utility supply as one source rather than the sole source. The proposed architecture combines grid supply, solar PV, lithium-ion battery energy storage, standby generators, automatic transfer/static switching, load criticality, protection and an energy-management system. Battery storage provides rapid ride-through and short-duration autonomy; solar reduces daytime fuel use and recharges storage; generators become controlled long-duration backup rather than continuously loaded prime sources. The framework emphasizes measured load profiles, N+1 thinking for critical backup, battery state-of-charge reserves, power-quality monitoring, black-start capability, preventive maintenance and lifecycle-cost optimization. Conclusion: Maximum border availability is achieved not by adding more generators but by engineering source diversity, fast storage, protected critical buses and disciplined control. Nigeria Customs should move from fragmented grid-generator-solar arrangements toward standardized, monitored hybrid microgrids designed around mission-critical loads and locally validated reliability targets.
records.keywords: energy resilience; hybrid microgrid; Nigeria Customs Service; land-border operations; solar photovoltaic; battery energy storage system; diesel generator; critical infrastructure; power quality; energy management system

records.title: Mathematical Modelling of Residential Electricity Demand for Peak-Load Reduction in Nigeria: A Demand-Response Optimisation Framework Calibrated to Dota Community, Gwagwalada
records.author_source_text: Abdulsalam A. Abdulrahman
records.abstract: Background: Nigeria’s electricity-access challenge is increasingly being addressed through grid reform and distributed renewable systems, but supply-side expansion does not by itself resolve concentrated residential peaks. The author’s prior Dota Community study reported a residential demand of 59.61 kWh/day and 9.62 kW peak, representing 57.43% of the community load. Objective: This study develops a transparent mathematical demand-response model that uses those aggregate values only as calibration anchors and asks a distinct question: how much peak demand can be redistributed when a defined share of household electricity use is time-flexible? Methods: A 24-hour residential archetype was reconstructed to preserve the reported daily energy and peak demand. Linear programming then shifted 10–40% of hourly demand within a bounded time window while conserving total energy. The primary objective minimized the daily maximum demand; secondary penalties represented a normalized time-of-use cost signal and shifting distance. Results: With 30% flexible demand and a ±3-hour shifting window, peak demand fell from 9.62 to 6.73 kW (30.0%), the peak-to-average ratio fell from 3.87 to 2.71, and load factor increased from 25.8% to 36.9%. The normalized cost index decreased by 9.2% with no reduction in daily energy. At 40% flexibility, peak demand fell to 5.77 kW and the cost index decreased by 12.2%. Sensitivity analysis showed that short shifting windows could achieve the same technical peak reduction in this calibrated case, while wider windows increased economic scheduling opportunity. Conclusion: Demand flexibility can complement solar-storage sizing and stochastic renewable-integration strategies in Nigerian households and mini-grids. The reported results are scenario-based technical potential—not measured behavioural response—and implementation depends on metering, controllable loads, consumer safeguards and locally validated tariffs.
records.keywords: demand response; residential electricity; mathematical optimisation; load shifting; peak demand; Nigeria; smart metering; mini-grids; Dota Community; energy flexibility

records.title: Design, Small-Signal Modeling and Prototype Implementation of a 24 V-to-19 V PWM Buck Converter with Type-III Voltage-Mode Compensation
records.author_source_text: CHIA, Shiaondo Kenneth¹*. AMENGER, Gbaden2; GOSHWE, N. Y.3; ¹ CHIA TECH Solutions and Resources Limited, Nigeria; original project investigator, Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi (2016); *Corresponding author: chiakenneth01@gmail.com · ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-6434-4586
records.abstract: Background: A 2016 engineering project at the Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi designed and implemented a pulse-width-modulated buck converter to step 24 V DC down to a regulated 19 V output. Objective: This article converts that archived project into a compact, publication-ready engineering paper, reconstructing the power-stage mathematics, voltage-mode feedback loop and Type-III compensation while preserving the documented prototype and simulation evidence. Methods: The archived specifications were audited and re-expressed using continuous-conduction-mode (CCM) equations, small-signal control-to-output modeling, K-factor pole-zero placement and analytical ripple calculations. The source specifies 24 V input, 19 V rated output, 3.5 A, 66.5 W, 30 kHz switching, L = 251 µH, C = 15 µF, capacitor ESR = 10 mΩ and inductor DCR = 2 mΩ. Results: The ideal duty ratio is 0.7917. At the 3.5 A design point the equivalent rated load is 5.43 Ω, while the archived simulation schematic separately uses a nominal 5 Ω test load. The reconstructed inductor ripple is approximately 0.526 A peak-to-peak (15.0% of rated output current), with an analytical output-ripple estimate of about 0.151 V peak-to-peak when capacitive and ESR terms are combined. The LC double-pole frequency is approximately 2.594 kHz and the capacitor-ESR zero approximately 1.061 MHz. The documented Type-III network (R1 = 2.2 kΩ, R2 = 5.9 kΩ, R3 = 38.8 Ω, C1 = 34.2 nF, C2 = 0.6 nF, C3 = 90 nF) is consistent with a voltage-mode compensation strategy that places two zeros around the LC resonance and high-frequency poles above the crossover region. Conclusion: The archived design is technically coherent at its rated point and demonstrates the engineering value of PWM, CCM energy transfer and Type-III loop shaping. The article also identifies legacy reporting inconsistencies that should not be interpreted as new measurements, notably the source wording that labels 19 V and 3.5 A as ripple values.
records.keywords: buck converter; DC-DC conversion; pulse-width modulation; voltage-mode control; Type-III compensation; K-factor; small-signal model; continuous conduction mode; power electronics

records.title: TECHNOLOGY · CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE REVIEW AND DESIGN FRAMEWORK
records.author_source_text: Prompting for Human-Centred Output: The HUMAN Framework for Credible, Context-Aware Generative AI Writing; CHIA Shiaondo Kenneth
records.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate writing, yet a fluent draft may remain generic, unsupported or misaligned with its reader. This conceptual practice review develops the HUMAN framework for credible and context-aware AI-assisted writing: Human intent and evidence; User and audience alignment; Message architecture; Authentic detail and accountability; and Natural revision and judgement. An integrative synthesis connected research on prompt design, human-AI co-writing, iterative refinement, hallucination and educational AI governance with the practical requirements of academic, professional and public communication. The synthesis shows that quality is created both upstream, by supplying verified source material and operational constraints, and downstream, through targeted human review. Surface instructions to 'sound human' cannot substitute for evidence, a real audience, a section-level purpose and accountable verification. The paper provides a nine-part prompt architecture, an editorial rubric and adoption controls covering privacy, attribution, bias, confidentiality and disclosure. The framework does not claim to detect AI authorship or to legitimise impersonation and detector evasion. It positions generative AI as a bounded drafting technology whose output becomes publishable only through human selection, verification and approval. Experimental validation across models, genres, languages and levels of writer expertise remains necessary.
records.keywords: prompt engineering; generative AI; human-AI collaboration; editorial quality; source grounding; responsible AI

records.title: Loss-Aware Reliability Analysis and Contemporary Re-Engineering of a 24 V-to-19 V, 66.5 W PWM Buck Converter: Component Stress, Efficiency Bounds and Validation Protocol
records.author_source_text: CHIA, Shiaondo Kenneth¹* · AMENGER, Gbaden² · GOSHWE, N. Y.³; ¹ CHIA TECH Solutions and Resources Limited, Nigeria; original project investigator, Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi (2016); ² Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria; original project investigator, Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi (2016); ³ Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi, Nigeria; project supervisor (2016); *Corresponding author: chiakenneth01@gmail.com · ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-6434-4586
records.abstract: Background: The archived 2016 project developed a 24 V-to-19 V pulse-width-modulated buck converter at 30 kHz with a 3.5 A, 66.5 W rated point, a 251 µH inductor, 15 µF output capacitor, 10 mΩ capacitor ESR and 2 mΩ inductor DCR. The report documents MATLAB/Simulink development, PWM waveforms and prototype implementation, and later states efficiency above 81%, but it does not preserve a complete part-specific loss budget or a traceable efficiency-test boundary. Objective: This study performs a distinct reliability-oriented re-analysis of the same engineering work, quantifying component current stress, reconstructable passive losses, semiconductor-loss sensitivity and the measurement requirements needed for a modern repeat build. Methods: Source parameters were preserved exactly. Continuous-conduction-mode equations were used to derive peak/RMS currents and ripple. Because MOSFET RDS(on), diode forward drop and switching transition times are not recoverable from the archive, they were treated as explicit sensitivity variables rather than invented historical measurements. Parametric efficiency surfaces and load sweeps were generated from transparent analytical assumptions. Results: The rated duty ratio is 0.7917 and the inductor ripple is 0.526 A p-p, giving Ipk = 3.763 A, IQ,rms = 3.117 A, ID,rms = 1.599 A and IC,rms = 0.152 A. The documented 2 mΩ inductor DCR contributes only about 24.55 mW copper loss and the 10 mΩ capacitor ESR about 0.23 mW at the rated point. Incremental loss sensitivity is approximately 0.097 W per additional 10 mΩ of MOSFET RDS(on), 0.073 W per 0.1 V of diode forward drop and 0.0126 W per additional 10 ns of combined switching transition. Even a deliberately conservative analytical stress case remains above 96% when only these modeled power-stage terms are included; therefore, the archived “>81%” statement cannot be reconstructed from the available component record alone. At 66.5 W output, exactly 81% efficiency would correspond to a 15.60 W total-loss ceiling, but the historical measurement boundary is unspecified. Conclusion: The design is a strong educational and engineering case study, but a contemporary efficiency or reliability claim should be based on a fresh parts audit, simultaneous input/output power measurement, loop-gain verification, calibrated ripple capture and thermal characterization. The paper preserves the historical prototype evidence while preventing analytical reconstructions from being misreported as new measurements.
records.keywords: buck converter; power loss; efficiency; component stress; reliability; thermal design; PWM; DC-DC conversion; failure-mode analysis; validation protocol

records.title: Control-Oriented Mathematical Review of a 24 V-to-19 V PWM Buck Converter: State-Space Averaging, CCM Boundary, Type-III Loop Compensation and Design Consistency
records.author_source_text: CHIA, Shiaondo Kenneth¹* · AMENGER, Gbaden² · GOSHWE, N. Y.³; ¹ CHIA TECH Solutions and Resources Limited, Nigeria; original project investigator, Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi (2016); ² Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria; original project investigator, Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi (2016); ³ Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi, Nigeria; project supervisor (2016); *Corresponding author: chiakenneth01@gmail.com · ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-6434-4586
records.abstract: Background: The archived 2016 project designed, simulated and implemented a 24 V-to-19 V voltage-mode PWM buck converter at 30 kHz using a 251 µH inductor, 15 µF output capacitor, 10 mΩ capacitor ESR and 2 mΩ inductor DCR. Its control design selected a 6 kHz crossover target, 60° desired phase margin and a Type-III compensator through a K-factor procedure. Objective: This paper provides a theory-centred re-analysis of the same converter, preserving the source record while reconstructing its switch-state equations, state-space averaged model, small-signal duty-to-output dynamics, CCM/DCM boundary, frequency landmarks and Type-III phase budget. It also audits mathematical inconsistencies that become visible when the archived equations are recomputed. Methods: Ideal CCM switching equations were averaged and linearized around the documented operating point. The rated 3.5 A condition was treated as the principal load case (R = 19/3.5 = 5.43 Ω), while the independently documented 5 Ω schematic load was retained as a separate source branch. Bode response, phase budget and K-factor sensitivity were computed analytically. Results: The ideal duty ratio is 0.7917, Ton = 26.39 µs and Toff = 6.94 µs. The formula-consistent inductor ripple is 0.526 A p-p, giving a CCM boundary current of about 0.263 A and Rcrit ≈ 72.3 Ω. The LC double-pole frequency is 2.594 kHz and the ESR zero is approximately 1.06 MHz. At the archived 6 kHz crossover, the ideal power-stage phase is approximately −158.2°. A 60° phase-margin target therefore requires about +38.2° compensator phase at crossover; when the Type-III integrator’s −90° baseline is included, the two lead sections must supply about 128.2° of lead, corresponding to K ≈ 18.9. The archived 150° boost gives K ≈ 57.7 and is therefore conservative but highly sensitive. The historical report also contains two explicit consistency issues: 3.5 A at 19 V implies 5.43 Ω rather than 5 Ω, and the displayed ripple equation uses Vout while its numerical substitution uses 24 V. Conclusion: The converter is theoretically coherent at the topology and loop-design level, but a modern publication benefits from separating the PWM modulator gain from LC-plant phase, distinguishing parallel source load cases and documenting arithmetic substitutions. The resulting framework is a stronger theoretical basis for simulation, frequency-response verification and future hardware replication.
records.keywords: buck converter; state-space averaging; small-signal model; voltage-mode control; Type-III compensation; K-factor; CCM; Bode plot; phase margin; power electronics

records.title: Coupled Mathematical Modelling of Building Envelope and Cooling-Efficiency Standards for Nigerian Multi-Unit Housing: An Abuja-Calibrated BEEC–SONMELS Predictive Scenario Framework
records.author_source_text: ABDULRAHMAN, Abdulsalam A.2 · CHIA, Shiaondo Kenneth1*; 1 CHIA TECH Solutions and Resources Limited, Nigeria; 2 Department of Building Technology, University of Abuja, Nigeria; *Corresponding author: chiakenneth01@gmail.com · ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-6434-4586; Co-author contact: Abdulsalam.abdulrahman@uniabuja.edu.ng
records.abstract: Background: Nigeria now has two complementary efficiency instruments that operate at different scales: the 2017 National Building Energy Efficiency Code (BEEC), which constrains building design and regulated loads, and the 2026 Standards Organisation of Nigeria Mandatory Energy Labeling Scheme (SONMELS), which classifies air-conditioner efficiency by the Nigeria Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio (NSEER). Their combined energy implication for multi-unit housing has not been expressed in a transparent mathematical crosswalk. Objective: This study couples the published Abuja-calibrated BEEC multi-unit apartment benchmark with current SONMELS cooling classes to quantify whole-building energy consequences under explicit cooling-service stress. Methods: The model uses the BEEC technical-study archetype of 1,200 m² with annual intensity components of 22 kWh/m² for lighting, 116 kWh/m² for cooling and 25 kWh/m² for water heating. The BEEC study reports 49% annual savings and 52% peak-load savings over regulated loads for the multi-unit benchmark. The 49% regulated-load result is reconstructed using the BEEC lighting-power-density change from 13 to 6 W/m², leaving a consistent residual cooling component. That component is then crosswalked to the SONMELS 1–5-star lower-bound NSEER thresholds (3.10, 3.60, 4.20, 4.95 and 5.80) under a cooling-service multiplier κ = 0.8–1.3. Results: The published business-as-usual archetype corresponds to 163 kWh/m²·year or 195.60 MWh/year. Reconstructing the BEEC benchmark gives 95.38 kWh/m²·year or 114.46 MWh/year, a 41.5% whole-site reduction when the unchanged 25 kWh/m² water-heating component is retained. After the BEEC package, movement from the 1-star analytical reference to the 5-star threshold reduces modeled site energy from 114.46 to 80.81 MWh/year, a further 29.4% reduction and 58.7% below the original archetype. Even under a 20% cooling-service stress (κ = 1.2), the BEEC + 5-star scenario remains at 88.54 MWh/year, 54.7% below the baseline. Conclusion: Building-envelope compliance and appliance efficiency are multiplicative rather than substitutable. The most resilient pathway for Nigerian multi-unit housing is to reduce cooling service demand through BEEC-compliant envelope and lighting measures before improving equipment efficiency through SONMELS. The results are a standards-coupled reanalysis of published and official evidence, not new field measurements.
records.keywords: building energy efficiency; BEEC; SONMELS; multi-unit housing; cooling; air conditioners; NSEER; mathematical modelling; Abuja; Nigeria

records.title: Antimicrobial Resistance Profiles of Clinical and Environmental Staphylococcus aureus Across Six Secondary Health-Care Centres in Taraba State, Nigeria: Laboratory Evidence and Contemporary AMR Implications
records.author_source_text: MELLAH, Iwanger1*; 1 Federal University of Agriculture, Makurdi, Nigeria; *Corresponding author: whoisdrmellah@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus remains a high-priority antimicrobial-resistance pathogen, while local clinical and environmental surveillance is essential for infection control. This article develops the first journal paper from a completed Medical Microbiology thesis by isolating its most internally coherent major finding: occurrence and phenotypic antimicrobial resistance of S. aureus across secondary health-care centres in Taraba State. Objective: To quantify S. aureus recovery and compare resistance patterns between clinical and hospital-environment isolates, while placing the completed experiments in contemporary 2024–2026 AMR evidence. Methods: Three hundred specimens were collected from six secondary health-care centres (50 per facility) across the Northern, Central and Southern senatorial zones. Clinical and environmental specimens underwent culture, Gram staining, catalase and coagulase testing; antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by agar disc diffusion using ciprofloxacin 5 µg, tetracycline 30 µg, erythromycin 15 µg, methicillin 5 µg, amoxicillin 30 µg, penicillin 10 µg, gentamicin 10 µg and ampicloxacillin 20 µg. The primary resistance endpoint uses the thesis resistance table, comprising 43 clinical and 17 environmental S. aureus isolates. Two-sided Fisher exact tests were recalculated from the reported resistance counts as a 2026 statistical update. Results: Gram/catalase screening yielded 189/300 (63.0%; 95% Wilson CI 57.4–68.3) presumptive Staphylococcus isolates. Coagulase testing identified 60/189 (31.7%; 95% CI 25.5–38.7) S. aureus, equivalent to 60/300 (20.0%; 95% CI 15.9–24.9) of all specimens. Wukari had the highest S. aureus yield (16/50; 32.0%) and Gembu the lowest (4/50; 8.0%). Across the 60 isolates, resistance was highest to penicillin (43/60; 71.7%), erythromycin (39/60; 65.0%), tetracycline (35/60; 58.3%) and ampicloxacillin (32/60; 53.3%), and lowest to gentamicin (8/60; 13.3%) and ciprofloxacin (10/60; 16.7%). Clinical versus environmental resistance was 69.8% versus 76.5% for penicillin, 69.8% versus 52.9% for erythromycin, and 23.3% versus 41.2% for methicillin. None of the eight source-group comparisons reached p<0.05 by Fisher exact test. Conclusion: The completed laboratory evidence demonstrates simultaneous clinical and environmental reservoirs of S. aureus and a substantial resistance burden, especially to penicillin, erythromycin, tetracycline and ampicloxacillin. The findings support facility-level antibiogram surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, environmental decontamination and modern molecular follow-up.

records.title: From AC Socket to Silicon: End-to-End Circuit Analysis of 65 W Modern Laptop Power Systems — A Comparative Study of HP, Dell and Lenovo Architectures
records.author_source_text: CHIA, Shiaondo Kenneth¹* · AMENGER, Gbaden²; ¹ CHIA TECH Solutions and Resources Limited, Nigeria; Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi, Nigeria; ² Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria; Department of Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi, Nigeria; *Corresponding author: chiakenneth01@gmail.com · ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-6434-4586
records.abstract: Background: Modern laptops are powered by a cascade of converters extending from universal AC mains through an isolated adapter, USB-C Power Delivery (PD), protected motherboard power paths, battery charging, always-on rails and high-current point-of-load regulators. Public documentation usually describes these blocks separately, making end-to-end circuit interpretation difficult. Objective: To develop and validate a unified circuit-level model of the complete laptop power chain and compare three common 65 W-class business platforms: HP ProBook 440 G10, Dell Latitude 5540 and Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 5. Methods: A comparative technical case-study was performed using official OEM adapter/battery specifications, USB-IF power-delivery requirements, and contemporary notebook reference designs from Texas Instruments. The authors derived the AC rectification, USB-PD power contract, input-path loss, NVDC buck-boost battery interface, CC-CV charging behavior, motherboard power-tree, multiphase CPU regulation and end-to-end loss equations. No proprietary motherboard schematic or undisclosed OEM measurement is claimed. Results: All three sample platforms converge on the 65 W class, with 20 V/3.25 A representing the dominant full-power USB-C operating point. At 230 V mains, the rectified peak is 325.3 V. A published 65 W GaN quasi-resonant adapter reference design reports 94.32% full-load efficiency at 230 V, implying about 68.9 W real input for 65 W DC output under that reference condition. The Dell sample documents an 11.4 V, 54 Wh three-cell battery, giving 4.74 Ah nominal energy capacity and an ideal 20 V-to-11.4 V buck duty ratio of about 0.57. The maximum listed batteries of the HP, Dell and Lenovo samples are 51, 54 and 57 Wh respectively. Conclusion: The modern laptop is best understood as a digitally negotiated, multi-stage power-conversion system rather than a single 19–20 V appliance. Reliable diagnosis and design require following energy, control and protection from the AC socket to the final sub-1.2 V silicon rails.

records.title: Molecular Virulence and Clonal Architecture of Clinical and Environmental Staphylococcus aureus in Taraba State, Nigeria: PVL, mecA, SCCmec and spa-Typing Evidence
records.author_source_text: MELLAH, Iwanger¹*; ¹ Federal University of Agriculture, Makurdi, Nigeria; *Corresponding author: whoisdrmellah@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Molecular surveillance is necessary to distinguish methicillin resistance, virulence and clonal spread within Staphylococcus aureus populations. This article develops the molecular-epidemiology findings of a completed six-hospital laboratory investigation in Taraba State, Nigeria. Methods: The parent study processed 300 clinical and hospital-environment specimens. Sixty coagulase-positive S. aureus isolates were obtained after culture and biochemical identification. Molecular work included PCR confirmation with the S. aureus-specific nuc target; detection of mecA and Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) targets; SCCmec characterization; and protein A (spa) typing, with Sanger sequencing of PCR products. Results: The thesis reports that all MRSA isolates carried mecA. One PVL-positive MRSA was assigned SCCmec I/spa t8439 and a second PVL-positive MRSA SCCmec IV/spa t8440; other MRSA were reported as non-typeable by the applied SCCmec assay. The two resolved spa fingerprints were 07-23-21-17-34-383-16-34-33-13 and 07-13-12-12-34-34-33-212, respectively. The thesis further reports dominance of spa-CC084 among clinical isolates. An archived virulence-gene table reported significant clinical-environmental contrasts, but its category counts are internally inconsistent with the 43-clinical/17-environmental isolate partition; those inferential values are therefore preserved as source-reported outputs rather than recalculated. Contemporary Nigerian whole-genome evidence now demonstrates additional PVL-positive MRSA lineages, including t657/ST772/SCCmec V and t4690/ST152/SCCmec Vc. Conclusion: The Taraba dataset documents genetically heterogeneous PVL-positive MRSA and illustrates why local spa/SCCmec surveillance should progress toward whole-genome sequencing with strict denominator and metadata control.
records.keywords: Staphylococcus aureus; MRSA; mecA; Panton-Valentine leukocidin; SCCmec; spa typing; molecular epidemiology; Taraba State; Nigeria

records.title: Renal Biochemical Signatures of Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension in Tertiary Antenatal Care in Enugu State, Nigeria: Electrolyte, Urea–Creatinine and Plasma-Protein Profiles
records.author_source_text: EMMANUEL, CEPHASKING OGBOTU¹*; ¹ Department of Biochemistry, Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi, Nigeria; original study investigator (research completed 2021); *Corresponding author: cephasking2021@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy remain a major maternal–fetal health problem in Nigeria, and renal involvement is clinically important because pre-eclampsia can alter renal perfusion, glomerular filtration and protein handling before conventional azotemia becomes prominent. Objective: To characterize serum electrolytes, nitrogenous-waste markers and plasma proteins in women with pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) compared with normotensive pregnant women across gestation, using the completed 2021 tertiary-hospital study as the primary evidence base and contemporary guidance for interpretation. Methods: The archived study recruited pregnant women aged 24–36 years attending the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital and Enugu State University Teaching Hospital. The listed analytic groups comprised 149 women: normotensive first trimester (n=30), normotensive second trimester (n=30), normotensive third trimester (n=30), hypertensive second trimester (n=30) and hypertensive third trimester (n=29). Serum Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, urea, creatinine, total protein, albumin and globulin were assessed by documented colorimetric/titrimetric methods. The source analysis used one- and two-way ANOVA, Duncan multiple-range testing and SPSS v24, with p<0.05 as significant. Results: The original analysis found no significant between-group differences in Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, urea or creatinine (all reported p>0.05), although urea and creatinine were numerically higher in the hypertensive third-trimester group than in the corresponding normotensive group. In contrast, total protein, albumin and globulin were significantly lower in hypertensive groups (p<0.05). Digitization of the archived figures places albumin at approximately 31.4 g/L in hypertensive second trimester and 27.7 g/L in hypertensive third trimester, versus approximately 43.6 and 40.4 g/L in trimester-matched normotensive groups. Conclusion: The completed cohort shows a biochemical phenotype dominated by plasma-protein depletion rather than overt electrolyte failure or statistically demonstrable azotemia. Contemporary interpretation requires caution: preserved serum creatinine and electrolytes do not exclude pre-eclamptic renal involvement, and the study did not quantify urine protein. Current practice should integrate blood pressure with urine protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio, serum creatinine and broader maternal-organ assessment.

records.title: From Antibiograms to Whole-Genome Surveillance: A Critical Review of Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus in Nigeria Across Clinical, Environmental and One Health Interfaces
records.author_source_text: MELLAH, Iwanger¹*; ¹ Federal University of Agriculture, Makurdi, Nigeria; *Corresponding author: whoisdrmellah@gmail.com
records.abstract: Background: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) remains a high-priority antimicrobial-resistance pathogen and an important cause of healthcare-, community- and livestock-associated infection. Nigeria now has an evidence base spanning classical antibiograms, targeted PCR, spa/SCCmec typing and, increasingly, whole-genome sequencing (WGS), yet these layers are rarely synthesized into a single surveillance pathway. Objective: To critically integrate Nigerian evidence on antimicrobial resistance, mecA/mecC-SCCmec architecture, Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), clonal diversity, environmental persistence and One Health transmission, while identifying the laboratory and policy transition required for contemporary surveillance. Review approach: This structured critical narrative review searched PubMed/PMC-indexed literature, publisher records, World Health Organization (WHO) reports and Nigerian AMR policy documents, prioritizing Nigerian studies and systematic reviews published through 30 August 2026. It is not presented as an exhaustive systematic review or meta-analysis. Synthesis: Nigeria exhibits marked MRSA heterogeneity across settings. Historical studies documented diverse spa backgrounds and PVL-positive strains; recent clinical WGS from Lagos identified a dominant PVL-positive t657/ST772/SCCmec V Bengal Bay lineage, whereas other Nigerian studies report ST152, ST8, mecC, heterogeneous SCCmec types, biofilm determinants and clinically important phenotype-genotype discordance. A 2025 Nigerian One Health meta-analysis estimated pooled mecA prevalence at 51% (95% CI 14-86%) across included resistance-gene studies, with substantial heterogeneity. Livestock, foods and hospital environments provide plausible connected reservoirs, reinforcing the need to link clinical microbiology with environmental and veterinary surveillance. Conclusion: Nigeria should move from isolated antibiograms and single-gene PCR toward a tiered national model in which standardized AST and targeted molecular confirmation feed referral WGS, interoperable metadata and One Health response. The country's 2024-2028 AMR National Action Plan provides a policy platform for this transition.

records.title: Renewable Energy and Sustainable Power Systems for Rural Farming Communities in Nigeria: Productive-Use Electrification, Agricultural Resilience and an Integrated Engineering Framework
records.author_source_text: AMENGER, Gbaden; Nigeria Customs Service, Ogun State Command, Nigeria
records.abstract: Background: Rural agricultural productivity in Nigeria is constrained by a persistent energy-access deficit, unreliable grid supply, high dependence on small petrol and diesel generators, and weak cold-chain and processing infrastructure. Renewable energy can therefore create development value only when electricity access is converted into productive energy services across irrigation, storage, processing and rural enterprise. Objective: This article critically synthesizes contemporary evidence on decentralized renewable energy for Nigerian farming communities and develops an engineering and implementation framework for reliable, productive-use electrification. Methods: A structured critical review was updated through September 2026 using peer-reviewed studies and authoritative policy and programme documents published mainly from 2020 to 2026, with foundational sources retained where they define established engineering practice. Evidence was prioritized from Nigeria, then Sub-Saharan Africa, and evaluated across technical reliability, agricultural productivity, economic viability, environmental safeguards and institutional feasibility. Results: Nigeria’s 2021 electricity access was about 60% nationally but only 26% in rural areas, leaving more than 85 million people without access. Evidence from northeast Nigeria shows that small solar-powered cold stores can reduce food losses while increasing horticultural sales and revenues. Rural mini-grid studies show strong gains in productive activity and reduced reliance on generators, although household-income effects are heterogeneous. Geospatial modelling indicates that financing productive-use equipment can lower the modelled levelized cost of off-grid electrification more strongly than conventional loan or capital-subsidy approaches. Solar irrigation, cold-chain systems, agro-processing loads, solar-battery mini-grids and context-appropriate biogas are the most immediately relevant technology pathways, but adoption is limited by capital cost, technical capacity, maintenance, water-resource risks, tariff design and fragmented energy-agriculture planning. Conclusion: The most effective rural-energy strategy is not technology deployment in isolation but an integrated productive-use system that begins with agricultural load and resource assessment, sizes hybrid power for reliability, couples energy finance with income-generating equipment, builds local maintenance capacity, governs water and data responsibly, and verifies outcomes such as uptime, crop loss reduction, income, energy cost and emissions. The proposed READF-N framework provides a practical pathway for engineering, financing and governing renewable energy as productive agricultural infrastructure in Nigeria.

records.title: HUMANITIES & SOCIAL SCIENCES · NORMATIVE POLICY REVIEW AND SAFEGUARDING FRAMEWORK
records.author_source_text: Responsible Digital Technology Adoption in Nigerian Secondary STEM Education: A Rights, Religious-Pluralism and Child-Safeguarding Framework; UKULE, Peter¹*; ¹Department of Christian Studies and Religious Communication, University of Abuja, Abuja, Nigeria; Corresponding author: rev.ukulepeter@gmail.com
records.abstract: Digital platforms, learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence may widen access to STEM resources, support teachers and enable new forms of inquiry. They may also collect children's data, mediate speech and belief, amplify bias, expose learners to harm or displace accountable human judgment. This normative policy review examines responsible adoption in Nigerian secondary STEM education through constitutional rights, child-rights standards, data-protection law, education policy and international ethical guidance. It proposes the RIGHTS framework: Rights and best interests; Inclusion and equitable access; Governance of data and vendors; Human agency and pedagogical purpose; Trust, transparency and contestability; and Safeguarding across the technology lifecycle. Religious pluralism is treated as a rights and professional-practice issue: public education should neither impose nor disparage belief, and digital systems should support age-appropriate inquiry without profiling, stereotyping or coercion. The framework specifies a pre-procurement assessment, proportionate data controls, accessibility and offline alternatives, human review of consequential outputs, reporting and remedy pathways, and periodic exit decisions. It is a legal-ethical and policy synthesis, not legal advice, an empirical survey or a theological adjudication. Nigerian schools and authorities should obtain competent legal and safeguarding review for particular deployments. Responsible innovation is defined not by tool novelty but by demonstrated educational value, lawful and minimal data use, child participation, pluralism, safety and accountable human control.

records.title: ENTREPRENEURSHIP & MANAGEMENT · POLICY AND MANAGEMENT REVIEW
records.author_source_text: Empowering Nigerian MSMEs through Finance, Technology and Capability: The SCALE Framework for Sustainable Industrial Development; CHIA Shiaondo Kenneth
records.abstract: Micro, small and medium enterprises are central to Nigerian livelihoods and production, yet policy discussion often treats finance, technology, management capability, markets and infrastructure as separate problems. This review synthesises official Nigerian enterprise statistics, finance-market studies, credit-infrastructure evidence, data-protection law and technology-adoption literature. It proposes the SCALE framework: Structured records and formalisation pathways; Capital suited to business need and cash flow; Adoption of useful and trustworthy technology; Linkages to customers, suppliers and support institutions; and Enabling infrastructure, capability and resilience. SCALE treats credit as one component of an enterprise system rather than a universal first intervention. It sequences basic transaction records and unit economics before more complex digital systems, aligns working-capital instruments with cash-conversion cycles, and links adoption decisions to measurable operating problems. It also addresses cyber risk, personal-data governance, gender and disability inclusion, business continuity and climate exposure. A staged implementation scorecard separates reach from use, business performance and causal impact. The paper does not update the 2017 national MSME census, estimate a current enterprise population or claim that the framework improves survival or employment. Published finance-gap estimates are reported with their study dates and definitions and should not be treated as interchangeable. SCALE is a testable management and policy architecture whose modules should be adapted by sector, firm maturity and location, then evaluated against explicit counterfactual and cost assumptions.
